introduction: These readings teach how to look at the world. The universe is a scroll, a book beside the book of Scripture, in which the attributes of God are written; the material world corresponds to the spiritual at every point, so that what is below has its form above and the things we see are symbols; ‘Abdu’l-Bahá hopes the earth may become a mirror of the Kingdom. And the same world, taken for the reality, is a mirage, a shadow, a vapour. The guide itself quotes Plato, Plotinus, the Hermetic 'as above, so below' and the Qur'an. All ninety-six quotations are read here beside ninety-six from elsewhere. Most stand alongside: the heavens that declare, Paul's 'things that are made', the Qur'an's portents, Augustine questioning the earth, the duke's sermons in stones, Emerson's 'every natural fact is a symbol', Blake's grain of sand, Hopkins, Hebrews on the earthly shadow of heavenly things, Plato's cave, Goethe's last chorus, the Dhammapada's bubble and mirage. Seven push back or add a side: Darwin's entangled bank, Keats on the unwoven rainbow, Tennyson's nature red in tooth and claw, Nietzsche's 'remain true to the earth', the man to whom a primrose was only a primrose, Whitman leaving the astronomer's lecture, and Kipling beside a remark about how East and West understand the world.
questions: What does it mean to call the world a book? Give an example of something in nature you have 'read'.
'Every material thing represents some spiritual idea.' Tennyson saw nature red in tooth and claw. What does that mirror?
The readings call the world both a mirror of the Kingdom and a mirage. How can it be both?
Darwin explained the entangled bank by laws; Keats feared that explaining the rainbow would unweave it. Does scientific explanation close the book of creation or open it?
‘Abdu’l-Bahá hopes the earth will become a mirror of heaven. What would have to change for that to be so?
One reading says the Easterner understands the world as a reflection better than the Westerner. How should such a generalization be weighed?

outside.why: A psalm reads the same scroll: the heavens declare the glory of God; day unto day uttereth speech.
Isaiah says: lift up your eyes on high, and behold who hath created these things.
Job says: ask now the beasts, and they shall teach thee; speak to the earth, and it shall teach thee.
Genesis says that God saw every thing that he had made, and behold, it was very good.
Shelley wrote that life, like a dome of many-coloured glass, stains the white radiance of eternity.
Byron wrote that words are things, and a drop of ink makes thousands think.
Paul says the invisible things of God are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made.
Shakespeare's exiled duke finds tongues in trees, books in the running brooks, sermons in stones.
The Qur'an says: in the earth are portents for those whose faith is sure.
Emerson put it as a principle: every natural fact is a symbol of some spiritual fact.
Paul asks: know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost?
The Lord's Prayer asks that God's will be done in earth, as it is in heaven.
Jesus said: let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works.
The Song of Songs says: the flowers appear on the earth; the time of the singing of birds is come.
A psalm exclaims: O Lord, how manifold are thy works; in wisdom hast thou made them all.
Jesus reasoned from one to the other: if I have told you earthly things and ye believe not, how shall ye believe heavenly things?
Hebrews says the earthly sanctuary serves as the example and shadow of heavenly things.
The Wisdom of Solomon says that by the greatness and beauty of the creatures the maker of them is seen.
Augustine asked the earth, the sea and the creeping things, and each answered: I am not he.
Moses was told to make everything after the pattern shewed him in the mount.
Whitman believed a leaf of grass is no less than the journey-work of the stars.
Mark says that without a parable Jesus spake not unto the crowds.
Blake would see a world in a grain of sand, and a heaven in a wild flower.
Plato's Timaeus calls time a moving image of eternity, made when the heaven was set in order.
Plato pictures prisoners watching shadows on a cave wall, unaware of what casts them.
Paul calls the observances of the old law a shadow of things to come.
Paul says that beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, we are changed into the same image.
Malachi promises that the Sun of righteousness shall arise with healing in his wings.
Leibniz held that each simple substance is a perpetual living mirror of the universe.
Tennyson wrote of one God, one law, one element, and one far-off divine event to which the whole creation moves.
John saw the holy city coming down from God out of heaven.
Goethe's Faust ends with a chorus: all things transitory but as symbols are sent.
Kipling wrote that East is East and West is West, though he added that neither counts when two strong men meet. Is a habit of mind the property of a hemisphere?
Tennyson held a flower from a wall and said that to understand it would be to know what God and man is.
Hebrews says the law had a shadow of good things to come, and not the very image.
Paul says: now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face.
Zhuangzi says the perfect man uses his mind as a mirror, which responds and does not retain.
Paul says that the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.
The Qur'an says the trust was offered to the heavens and the earth, and man assumed it.
James says that every good gift is from above, from the Father of lights.
The Qur'an says: We shall show them Our portents on the horizons and within themselves.
Augustine approved of singing in church because by the delights of the ear the mind may rise to devotion.
Shakespeare's Lorenzo distrusts the man that hath no music in himself, nor is moved with concord of sweet sounds.
Dante saw the turning heavens moved by love: the Love which moves the sun and the other stars.
Wordsworth claimed that one impulse from a vernal wood may teach more of man than all the sages can.
A psalm calls on sun and moon and all the stars of light to praise their maker.
This is the Qur'an's verse: in the creation of the heavens and the earth are signs for people who have sense.
John saw a river of the water of life, and beside it the tree of life with leaves for the healing of the nations.
Ephesians calls: awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee light.
Darwin contemplated an entangled bank and saw forms produced by laws acting around us. Does nature symbolize, or simply happen?
Keats feared that philosophy would unweave the rainbow, once we know her woof and texture. Does explaining a thing end its meaning?
Hopkins wrote that the world is charged with the grandeur of God.
Micah foresees a day when each sits under his vine and fig tree, and none makes them afraid.
Isaiah says the wilderness shall be glad, and the desert shall rejoice, and blossom as the rose.
Ecclesiastes says that to every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven.
Ezekiel saw breath enter dry bones, and they lived, and stood upon their feet.
Jesus said that men do not put new wine into old bottles.
Hosea hears God say of his people: my people are destroyed for lack of knowledge.
Jesus told his followers: ye are the light of the world; a city on a hill cannot be hid.
Micah sums up what is required: to do justly, to love mercy, to walk humbly with thy God.
A psalm says: how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity.
Longfellow says our destined end is to act, that each tomorrow find us farther than today.
Jesus told the Pharisees to cleanse first that which is within the cup, that the outside may be clean also.
Juvenal said one should pray for a sound mind in a sound body.
Paul told the Athenians that in God we live, and move, and have our being.
Isaiah has God say that his word shall not return void, but prosper in the thing whereto he sent it.
Elizabeth Barrett Browning wrote that earth is crammed with heaven, and every common bush afire with God.
Wordsworth describes a man to whom a primrose by the river was a yellow primrose, and nothing more. What does it take to see more?
Samuel is told that man looketh on the outward appearance, but the Lord looketh on the heart.
Tennyson saw nature red in tooth and claw. If the earthly realm mirrors the heavenly, what does predation mirror?
Shakespeare's Prospero calls the towers and palaces an insubstantial pageant, and us such stuff as dreams are made on.
A psalm says that every man walketh in a vain shew, and is disquieted in vain.
Jesus told his disciples that their sorrow would be turned into joy.
Paul calls his troubles a light affliction, which is but for a moment.
The image is the Qur'an's: a mirage in a desert, which the thirsty one supposes to be water.
The Dhammapada says: look upon the world as a bubble, look upon it as a mirage.
James asks what our life is: a vapour that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away.
Shelley wrote of a dead poet that he hath awakened from the dream of life.
Nietzsche's Zarathustra conjures his hearers to remain true to the earth. Is calling the world a shadow a way of seeing it truly, or of leaving it?
The Preacher begins his book: vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher; all is vanity.
Jesus said: lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt.
Paul says to use this world as not abusing it, for the fashion of this world passeth away.
Whitman left the astronomer's proofs and columns and looked up in perfect silence at the stars. Are the sciences one of the two books, or a commentary on it?
Jesus said the kingdom comes not with observation: behold, the kingdom of God is within you.
Jesus compared the kingdom of heaven to a grain of mustard seed.
The Qur'an says that though the sea became ink for the words of the Lord, it would be used up first.
Jesus compared the kingdom to leaven hidden in three measures of meal, till the whole was leavened.
Plato says the good gives being to what is known, as the sun gives growth to what is seen.
Emerson saw one figure, the circle, repeated without end through nature, the highest emblem in the cipher of the world.
Whitman said: I find letters from God dropt in the street, and every one is signed by God's name.
The Qur'an points to vineyards and date-palms, like and unlike, watered with one water.
Paul says the eternal power of God is understood by the things that are made.
Plotinus pictures what proceeds from the One as light encircling the sun.
The Qur'an calls the life of this world but comfort of illusion.
The Qur'an likens the life of the world to rain that greens the earth, and then it is stubble.
Confucius asked: does Heaven speak? The four seasons pursue their courses, and all things are produced.

exodus-pattern-shewed-in-the-mount.text: And look that thou make them after their pattern, which was shewed thee in the mount

wisdom-maker-of-them-is-seen.text: For by the greatness and beauty of the creatures proportionably the maker of them is seen
wisdom-maker-of-them-is-seen.caveat: From the Apocrypha of the King James Bible; Catholic and Orthodox Christians count the book in the Old Testament.

dhammapada-bubble-mirage.text: Look upon the world as a bubble, look upon it as a mirage: the king of death does not see him who thus looks down upon the world

goethe-all-things-transitory.text: All things transitory / But as symbols are sent: / Earth’s insufficiency / Here grows to Event
goethe-all-things-transitory.author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
